# Collaborative Science with GitHub

In the last chapter, we covered how Git works locally on your own computer.
Now we'll connect that local repository to GitHub, which lets you back up
your work remotely and collaborate with others.

A **remote repository** is a copy of your repository stored somewhere other
than your own computer — in our case, on GitHub's servers. Most commonly,
you'll have a **local repository** on your machine and a **remote
repository** on GitHub that mirrors it. Keeping the two synchronized is what
lets you collaborate: your changes get pushed up to GitHub, and your
collaborators' changes get pulled down to your machine.

There are two ways to set up a local-remote pair. You can start with a
local repository and connect it to a new, empty remote — this is the
approach you already used when you set up your course textbook repo. Or you
can start with a repository that already exists on GitHub and download
("clone") a copy of it to your computer — useful when joining a project
that someone else already started.

## Adding a remote to a local repository

If you already have a Git repository on your computer (created with
`git init`), you can connect it to a GitHub repository by adding a
**remote** — essentially, a saved address pointing to where the remote copy
lives.

First, create an empty repository on GitHub: click the **+** icon in the
top-right corner of any GitHub page and select **New repository**. Give it
a name — often the same name as your local folder, for consistency, though
this isn't required. Leave the repository completely empty: don't add a
README, `.gitignore`, or license through GitHub's interface. If the remote
repository already has content when you try to connect it to your local
one, Git will see them as conflicting and won't be able to link them
cleanly.

Once created, GitHub will show you the repository's URL. Copy it, then run
the following in your terminal (from inside your local repository folder):

```
git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git
```

`origin` is the conventional name for a repository's primary remote.
Technically you could name it anything, but since GitHub defaults to
`origin` and virtually every Git tutorial assumes this name, there's rarely
a good reason to deviate from it.

To confirm the remote was added correctly:

```
git remote -v
```

A repository can have multiple **branches** — we'll cover what that means
later in this chapter — but every repository has at least one, its default
or "main" branch. Make sure yours is named `main` (rather than the older
default name, `master`):

```
git branch -M main
```

## Pushing to a remote repository

**Pushing** transfers an exact copy of your local repository's files up to
the remote. The first time you push a given branch, it's standard to also
tell Git which remote branch your local branch should sync with going
forward, using the `-u` (upstream) flag:

```
git push -u origin main
```

Here, `main` refers to the name of the branch you're pushing — right now,
it's the only branch that exists in your repository, so there's no
ambiguity yet. (Later in this chapter, you'll learn that a repository can
have multiple branches. When that's the case, each one can be pushed and
synced independently — but for now, just know that `main` is what your one
branch happens to be called.)

The `-u` flag tells Git to remember the pairing between your local `main`
branch and the remote `main` branch on `origin`. Once that pairing is set,
future pushes to this branch can just be `git push`, with no need to
specify `origin main` every time.

This only needs to be done once per branch. After that, pushing new commits
is as simple as:

```
git push
```

You'll be prompted to authenticate the first time you push. GitHub does 
not accept your account password for this — instead, you'll need a 
**Personal Access Token (PAT)**, a long string of characters that functions 
like a password specifically for command-line operations like this one.

To generate one: on GitHub, click your profile picture (top right) →
**Settings** → scroll to the bottom of the left sidebar → **Developer
settings** → **Personal access tokens** → **Tokens (classic)** →
**Generate new token** → **Generate new token (classic)**. Give it a
name, set an expiration date, and check the box for the **repo** scope
(this grants push/pull access to your repositories). Click **Generate
token**, then copy it immediately — GitHub will only show it to you once.

When prompted for a username, enter your GitHub username. When prompted for
a password, paste your token instead of your actual account password.

Once you push, your local and remote repositories mirror each other. From
here on, your everyday workflow gains one more step: **add, commit, push.**

## Cloning a repository

The other way to set up a local-remote pair is to create the repository on
GitHub first, then **clone** it — download a full copy — onto your
computer. In this case, the remote repository doesn't need to be empty; in
fact, it's common to include a README when creating it this way.

Cloning is especially useful for joining a project someone else already
started. If you're added as a collaborator on their repository, cloning
gives you a local copy that stays synchronized with the shared remote.

To clone their repository, navigate to the folder where you want the copy to
live, then run:

```
git clone https://github.com/their-username/their-repo.git
```

Git will create a new folder (named after the repository) containing a full
copy of the project, already connected to the remote as `origin`.

## Synchronizing changes among collaborators

The reverse of pushing is **pulling** — downloading changes from the remote
repository into your local copy:

```
git pull
```

When collaborating, you'll pull periodically to stay synchronized with
whatever your collaborators have pushed. You'll also need to pull before
you push your own changes whenever the remote has commits your local copy
doesn't — Git won't let you push otherwise. If your local and remote copies
are already in sync, running `git pull` simply does nothing.

If a collaborator has changed the same part of a file you've also changed,
pulling will trigger a **merge conflict**, which Git can't resolve
automatically.

## Resolving conflicts

Merge conflicts are a normal, expected part of collaborative work — not a
sign that something has gone wrong. If you try to push while the remote has
changes you don't have locally, you'll see something like:

```
! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/username/repo.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing
hint: to the same ref. You may want to first integrate the remote changes
hint: (e.g., 'git pull ...') before pushing again.
```

To resolve this, pull the latest changes, merge them with your own, and
push the result.

When you pull and there's a genuine conflict — the same lines of a file
edited differently by two people — Git won't silently pick one version over
the other. Instead, it marks the conflicting section directly inside the
file, showing both versions separated by a line of `=` signs, with markers
indicating where each version begins and ends.

From there, it's up to you to decide how to reconcile the conflict: keep
your version, keep your collaborator's, write something new that combines
both, or remove the change entirely. Once you've edited the file to remove
the conflict markers and saved it, continue as normal: stage it, commit it,
and push. The next time your collaborators pull, they'll receive the
resolved version.

It's worth noting that a merge conflict doesn't require the two edits to
actually contradict each other — any time two people edit the *same line*
of the *same file* around the same time, Git flags it as a conflict to be
safe, even if the changes could technically coexist. Resolving it just
means confirming, by hand, whether both edits should be kept.

## Avoiding conflicts

Since resolving a conflict always requires a human judgment call, it's
generally better to avoid them in the first place. A few habits help:

- **Pull often** — the more current your local copy is, the less likely
  your changes will collide with someone else's.
- **Make small, frequent commits** — smaller changes are less likely to
  overlap with a collaborator's edits than large, infrequent ones.
- **Keep code organized into smaller, focused files** — reduces the odds
  that two people are working in the same file at the same time.
- **Divide project tasks along clear lines of ownership** — agree as a team
  on who leads which piece of the project (e.g., one person owns the data
  cleaning script, another owns the visualization script, another owns the
  statistical analysis), so that any given file is normally being edited by
  only one person at a time.
- **Use branches or forks** for larger or more experimental changes — more
  on this next.

Dividing work this way is often the single most effective way to avoid
conflicts, since most merge conflicts happen when two people edit the same
file around the same time. If your project's structure naturally routes
each collaborator into their own file or folder, conflicts become the
exception rather than the norm. This doesn't mean collaborators can't ever
touch the same file — just that it's worth having an explicit conversation
about ownership early on, rather than letting it happen by accident.

## Working with branches

By default, a repository has a single branch — its main branch. But you can
create additional branches to work on changes in isolation. Think of a
branch as a parallel version of your project: any commits you make on that
branch exist only there, without affecting the main branch, until you
choose to merge them back in.

Branches are especially useful for trying out significant changes without
risking your main, working version of the project. Let's say you submitted
your manuscript to a journal for peer review, and Reviewer 2 is asking for
changes you're not sure you agree with. You could create a new branch to
try out their suggested changes. If you like the result, you merge the
branch back into your main manuscript; if not, you simply delete the branch
and your original version is untouched.

To create a new branch:

```
git branch my-branch
```

To switch to it:

```
git checkout my-branch
```

Or do both in a single command:

```
git checkout -b my-branch
```

(the `-b` flag stands for "branch").

To confirm which branch you're currently on, `git log` will show `HEAD` —
a pointer indicating your current position — next to the relevant branch.

A new branch starts out sharing the same commit history as the branch it
was created from; after that point, the two histories can diverge freely.
Changes committed to your branch have no effect on the main branch until
you merge them:

```
git merge my-branch
```

Once merged, you can delete the branch if it's no longer needed:

```
git branch -d my-branch
```

If the two branches have conflicting changes, merging will trigger the same
kind of merge conflict discussed earlier, which you'll resolve the same
way.

## Forking a repository

**Forking** creates your own copy of someone else's repository on your
GitHub account, which you're free to modify without affecting their
original. This is different from cloning: forking happens on GitHub itself
first, creating a new remote repository under your own account, which you
can then clone locally if you want a working copy on your computer.

Forking is especially useful for contributing to a project you don't own —
for example, building on someone's published code, or proposing a change to
an open-source tool.

Unlike everything else in this chapter, forking is a GitHub feature, not a
Git command — there's no way to fork from the terminal. To fork a
repository, go to its page on GitHub and click **Fork** in the top-right
corner. This creates a copy under your own account.

If you also want a local copy, clone your fork the same way you'd clone any
other repository:

```
git clone https://github.com/your-username/forked-repo.git
```

To keep your fork up to date with the original repository (often called the
**upstream** repository), add it as an additional remote:

```
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-owner/original-repo.git
```

This lets you pull in any updates the original author makes. You won't be
able to push directly to their repository unless they've added you as a
collaborator — pull requests (next section) are how you propose changes
back to them instead.

## Pull requests

A **pull request** is how you propose merging your changes — whether from a
branch or a fork — into someone else's repository (or into your project's
main branch, if you're working with collaborators). If you're contributing
to someone else's project via a fork, a pull request is the only way to
have your changes considered for inclusion; you have no direct write access
to their repository. If you're a collaborator working within a shared
repository, you technically could merge your own changes directly — but
submitting a pull request is still good practice, since it gives your
collaborators a chance to review your changes before they become part of
the shared history.

To open a pull request, you'll need some committed changes on the branch or
fork you want merged. From the repository's page on GitHub, click the
**Pull requests** tab, then **New pull request**. Choose the branch you
want to merge, add a title and description explaining your changes, and
submit it. From there, anyone with access can comment on the pull request,
review the specific changes, and see the full list of commits it includes.

Once everyone involved is satisfied with the proposed changes and there are
no conflicts, the pull request can be merged with a single click.

## In-Class Activity: Practicing GitHub Collaboration

For this activity, pair up with a classmate. You'll take turns playing the
role of "repository owner" and "collaborator" so everyone experiences both
sides of a collaborative workflow — including resolving a merge conflict on
purpose.

### Part 1: Set up a shared repository

1. One partner (the **owner**) creates a new, empty repository on GitHub
   (don't add a README, `.gitignore`, or license).
2. The owner goes to the repository's **Settings > Collaborators** and adds
   the other partner as a collaborator. The collaborator will need to
   accept the invitation (usually sent by email or visible under their
   GitHub notifications).
3. The **collaborator** clones the repository to their own computer:

   ```
   git clone https://github.com/owner-username/repo-name.git
   ```

4. The **owner** creates a local repository on their own computer (using
   `git init` in a new folder, or reusing an existing local repo they'd
   like to connect), adds a file called `team-notes.md` with a sentence of
   any text, then adds the remote, stages, commits, and pushes:

   ```
   git remote add origin https://github.com/owner-username/repo-name.git
   git branch -M main
   git add .
   git commit -m "Add team notes file"
   git push -u origin main
   ```

### Part 2: Synchronize changes

5. The **collaborator** pulls the owner's changes:

   ```
   git pull
   ```

   Confirm `team-notes.md` now appears in their local copy.

6. The **collaborator** adds a new sentence to `team-notes.md`, then stages,
   commits, and pushes their edit.

7. The **owner** pulls to receive the collaborator's edit and confirms it
   appears in their local copy.

### Part 3: Create and resolve a merge conflict (on purpose)

8. **Without pulling first**, both partners simultaneously edit the *same
   line* of `team-notes.md` on their own computers (agree ahead of time on
   which line).

9. Whoever pushes **first** should succeed normally. Whoever pushes
   **second** will get a rejected push error, similar to what's shown
   earlier in this chapter.

10. The second person pulls, and should see conflict markers appear
    directly inside `team-notes.md`. Work together to resolve the conflict
    by editing the file to keep, combine, or discard the two versions, then
    stage, commit, and push the resolved file.

11. The first partner pulls one more time to confirm they now see the
    merged, conflict-free version.

### What to submit

As a pair, submit a short paragraph (3–5 sentences) describing what the
conflict markers looked like inside the file, and how you decided to
resolve the conflict.
